title: Personalpronomen und das Verb „sein“
summary: You'll be able to introduce yourself and others: name, origin, job, age and how you feel.
key_points: Personal pronouns: `ich`, `du`, `er/sie/es`, `wir`, `ihr`, `sie/Sie`.
`sein` is irregular: `ich bin`, `du bist`, `er ist`, `wir sind`, `ihr seid`, `sie/Sie sind`.
`du`/`ihr` for friends, family and children; `Sie` (always with a capital S) for formal situations.
Use `sein` for name, origin (`aus`), job (no article), age (`… Jahre alt`) and feelings.

blocks.text: Personal pronouns replace a name: *Anna* → `sie`, *Tom* → `er`. German has **three** ways to say *you*: `du`, `ihr` and `Sie`.
`ich` is written with a small letter (unlike English *I*) – except at the start of a sentence. Formal `Sie` is **always** capitalised.
`sein` is the most important verb in German – and it is **irregular**. Learn the forms by heart.
`wir`, `sie` and `Sie` always share the same form: `sind`.

blocks.why: `ihr` (you, plural) takes `seid`. Don't mix up `seid` (are) with `seit` (since) – they sound the same.

blocks.text: Use `du` (one person) and `ihr` (several people) with family, friends, children and often with colleagues. Use `Sie` with adults you don't know well: in shops, at the doctor's, in an office. `Sie` is the same for one person or many.

items.de: Hallo Lena, wie alt bist du?
items.en: Hi Lena, how old are you?

items.de: Kinder, seid ihr fertig?
items.en: Kids, are you ready?

items.de: Frau Weber, sind Sie Lehrerin?
items.en: Ms Weber, are you a teacher?

blocks.wrong: Herr Braun, bist Sie aus Berlin?
blocks.right: Herr Braun, sind Sie aus Berlin?
blocks.why: Formal `Sie` always takes the plural verb form `sind` – even when you talk to just one person.

blocks.text: Three times *sie*: `sie ist` = she is, `sie sind` = they are, `Sie sind` = you are (formal). The verb and the capital S tell you which one is meant.

items.de: Ich bin Anna.
items.en: I am Anna.
items.note: name (you can also say: Ich heiße Anna.)

items.de: Wir sind aus Italien.
items.en: We are from Italy.

items.de: Er ist Lehrer.
items.en: He is a teacher.

items.de: Ich bin 30 Jahre alt.
items.en: I am 30 years old.

items.de: Bist du müde?
items.en: Are you tired?

blocks.why: Age needs `alt` at the end. And never say *Ich habe 25 Jahre* – in German you *are* your age.
When you simply say what someone's job is, German uses no article: *She is a doctor* = `Sie ist Ärztin.`

blocks.text: Many jobs add `-in` for women: `Lehrer` → `Lehrerin`, `Arzt` → `Ärztin`, `Student` → `Studentin`.

exercises.en: I am Anna.
exercises.explain: With `ich` the form of sein is `bin`.

exercises.q: Das ist Tom. ___ ist aus England.
exercises.en: This is Tom. He is from England.
exercises.explain: Tom is a man, so the pronoun is `er` (he).

exercises.en: Kids, are you tired?
exercises.explain: `ihr` (you, plural) takes `seid`.

exercises.en: Excuse me, are you Mr Schmidt?
exercises.explain: Formal `Sie` always takes `sind`, even for one person.

exercises.en: I am 25 years old.
exercises.explain: Age is always `… Jahre alt`.

exercises.en: You are very nice.
exercises.explain: `du` → `bist`.

exercises.en: Maria is a doctor.
exercises.explain: Maria = `sie` (she) → `ist`. No article before the job.

exercises.en: We are from Poland.
exercises.explain: `wir` → `sind`.

exercises.q: ___ seid aus Wien, oder? (you, plural – informal)
exercises.en: You are from Vienna, right?
exercises.explain: `seid` is the form for `ihr`. It starts the sentence, so it's capitalised: `Ihr`.

accept: Student bin ich.
exercises.en: I am a student.
exercises.explain: The verb `bin` is in position 2. No article before the job.

exercises.en: Where are you from?
exercises.explain: Question word first, then the verb, then the subject: `Woher sind Sie?`

exercises.en: Lena is seven years old.
exercises.explain: Subject + `ist` + age + `Jahre alt`.

title: Verben im Präsens
title_en: Regular verbs in the present tense
summary: You'll be able to use regular verbs in the present tense to talk about what you do now, usually and soon.
key_points: Verb = stem + ending: `wohn-en` → `ich wohne`, `du wohnst`, `er wohnt`.
The endings are: `-e`, `-st`, `-t`, `-en`, `-t`, `-en`.
Stems in -t/-d add an extra `-e-`: `du arbeitest`, `er arbeitet`. Stems in -s/-ß/-z only add `-t` for du: `du heißt`, `du tanzt`.
There is only one present tense: `ich arbeite` = I work / I am working / I'm going to work.

blocks.text: The dictionary form of a verb is the **infinitive**. It almost always ends in `-en`: `wohnen`, `kommen`, `lernen`. Take away `-en` and you have the **stem**: `wohn-`, `komm-`, `lern-`. Then you add an ending that matches the person.
`wir`, `sie` and `Sie` look exactly like the infinitive. `er/sie/es` and `ihr` share the ending `-t`.

items.de: Ich wohne in Hamburg.
items.en: I live in Hamburg.

items.de: Er kommt aus Spanien.
items.en: He comes from Spain.

items.de: Wir lernen Deutsch.
items.en: We are learning German.

items.de: Spielt ihr gern Fußball?
items.en: Do you like playing football?

blocks.why: The `du` form always ends in `-st`.

blocks.text: Stems ending in **-t** or **-d** (`arbeit-`, `find-`) need an extra `-e-` before `-st` and `-t` – otherwise you couldn't pronounce them.

Stems ending in **-s, -ß** or **-z** (`reis-`, `heiß-`, `tanz-`) already end in an s-sound. So the `du` form only adds `-t`: `du reist`, `du heißt`, `du tanzt`. It looks the same as the er/sie/es form.

blocks.why: The stem `arbeit-` ends in -t, so you need `-et` for er/sie/es.
The stem `heiß-` already ends in an s-sound, so `du` only adds `-t`.

blocks.text: English has *I work*, *I am working* and *I do work*. German has just one form: `ich arbeite`. There is no -ing form. The present tense is also used for the future when a time word makes it clear.

items.de: Ich koche.
items.en: I cook. / I am cooking.

items.de: Was machst du? – Ich lerne Deutsch.
items.en: What are you doing? – I'm learning German.

items.de: Morgen spielen wir Tennis.
items.en: We're playing tennis tomorrow.
items.note: time word + present = future; the verb stays in position 2

items.de: Am Samstag kochen wir zusammen.
items.en: On Saturday we're going to cook together.

blocks.why: Don't translate *am* from *I am learning*. The German verb alone already means *am learning*.

blocks.text: To talk about the future, just add a time word: `morgen`, `heute Abend`, `am Montag`, `nächste Woche`.

exercises.en: I live in Berlin.
exercises.explain: `ich` → ending `-e`: `ich wohne`.

exercises.en: We are learning German.
exercises.explain: `wir` → ending `-en`, the same as the infinitive.

exercises.en: What's your name?
exercises.explain: The stem `heiß-` ends in an s-sound, so `du` only adds `-t`: `du heißt`.

exercises.en: He works in a café.
exercises.explain: Stem ending in -t → extra `-e-`: `er arbeitet`. (`arbeitest` is the du form.)

exercises.en: I'm going to play tennis tomorrow.
exercises.explain: German uses the simple present for the future: `ich spiele`. There's no extra *bin*.

exercises.en: You understand German well.
exercises.explain: `du` → ending `-st`: `du verstehst`.

exercises.en: You dance very well.
exercises.explain: `ihr` → ending `-t`: `ihr tanzt`.

exercises.en: Paul works every day.
exercises.explain: Paul = er. Stem `arbeit-` ends in -t, so add `-et`: `arbeitet`.

exercises.en: Do you like the music?
exercises.explain: Stem `find-` ends in -d → `du findest`. It starts the question, so it's capitalised.

accept: Deutsch lerne ich.
exercises.en: I'm learning German.
exercises.explain: The verb is in position 2. *I'm learning* is just `ich lerne`.

exercises.en: Where does Maria live?
exercises.explain: Question word, verb, subject. No *does* in German.

accept: Wir spielen morgen Fußball.
Fußball spielen wir morgen.
exercises.en: We're playing football tomorrow.
exercises.explain: Present tense + time word = future. The verb stays in position 2, so after `Morgen` comes `spielen`, then `wir`.

title: „haben“ und Verben mit Vokalwechsel
title_en: 'haben' (to have) and verbs with a vowel change
summary: You'll be able to use haben and common verbs like sprechen, lesen and fahren correctly in all persons.
key_points: `haben`: `ich habe`, `du hast`, `er hat`, `wir haben`, `ihr habt`, `sie haben`.
Some verbs change their stem vowel: e → i (`sprechen`), e → ie (`lesen`), a → ä (`fahren`).
The change happens **only** with `du` and `er/sie/es` – never with `ich`, `wir`, `ihr`, `sie/Sie`.
`wissen` and `mögen` are special: `ich weiß` / `er weiß`, `ich mag` / `er mag`.

blocks.text: `haben` is irregular only in the `du` and `er/sie/es` forms: the **b** disappears. All other forms follow the normal pattern.

items.de: Ich habe Hunger.
items.en: I'm hungry.

items.de: Hast du heute Zeit?
items.en: Do you have time today?

items.de: Sie hat zwei Kinder.
items.en: She has two children.

blocks.why: Hunger, thirst and time are things you *have* in German: `Hunger haben`, `Durst haben`, `Zeit haben`.
The er/sie/es form of haben is `hat`. `habt` is for `ihr`.

blocks.text: Some verbs change the vowel of their stem – but **only** in the `du` and `er/sie/es` forms. The endings stay completely regular.
Only the **two singular forms in the middle** of the table change: `du` and `er/sie/es`. `ich` and all plural forms keep the normal vowel.

blocks.why: The vowel change never happens with `ich`.
`ihr` is plural – no vowel change. Only `du fährst` and `er fährt` have ä.

blocks.text: Watch out: `essen` → `du isst` and `lesen` → `du liest` (the stem already has an s-sound, like `heißen`). `nehmen` → `du nimmst`, `er nimmt` (the h disappears, the m doubles).

items.de: Er spricht gut Deutsch.
items.en: He speaks German well.

items.de: Isst du gern Pizza?
items.en: Do you like eating pizza?

items.de: Lisa liest ein Buch.
items.en: Lisa is reading a book.

items.de: Das Baby schläft.
items.en: The baby is sleeping.

blocks.text: Good dictionaries show the change: *fahren (fährt)*, *sehen (sieht)*. Learn these verbs together with their er-form.

sections.heading: Two more special verbs: wissen and mögen

blocks.text: `wissen` (to know a fact) and `mögen` (to like) have special singular forms. Note that `ich` and `er/sie/es` are the same and have **no ending**.

items.de: Ich weiß es nicht.
items.en: I don't know.

items.de: Ich mag Katzen.
items.en: I like cats.

blocks.why: `ich weiß` and `er weiß` have no ending. Only `du weißt` has -t.

blocks.text: For a polite *I would like*, use `möchten`: `ich möchte`, `du möchtest`, `er/sie/es möchte`, `wir möchten`, `ihr möchtet`, `sie/Sie möchten`. Example: `Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.`

exercises.en: Do you have time today?
exercises.explain: `du` → `hast`. The b disappears.

exercises.en: Anna speaks English well.
exercises.explain: Anna = sie → e changes to i: `spricht`. (`sprecht` is the ihr form, `sprichst` the du form.)

exercises.en: I like reading books.
exercises.explain: No vowel change with `ich`: `ich lese`.

exercises.en: We're going to Vienna tomorrow.
exercises.explain: `wir` → no vowel change: `wir fahren`.

exercises.en: I don't know that.
exercises.explain: `ich weiß` – no ending. (`weißt` is du, `wisst` is ihr.)

exercises.en: You have two children.
exercises.explain: `ihr` → `habt`, regular ending -t.

exercises.en: What are you eating?
exercises.explain: e → i in the du form, and the s-sound stem only adds -t: `du isst`.

exercises.en: The baby is still sleeping.
exercises.explain: Das Baby = es → a changes to ä: `schläft`.

exercises.en: He takes a coffee.
exercises.explain: `nehmen` → `er nimmt`: e → i, the h disappears and the m doubles.

accept: Hunger habe ich.
exercises.en: I'm hungry.
exercises.explain: In German you *have* hunger: `Hunger haben`.

exercises.en: Do you speak German?
exercises.explain: Yes/no question: verb first. `du` → `sprichst` (e → i).

accept: Am Abend liest Lisa Zeitung.
Zeitung liest Lisa am Abend.
exercises.en: Lisa reads the newspaper in the evening.
exercises.explain: The verb `liest` (e → ie) is in position 2.

title: Nomen, Genus und Artikel
summary: You'll be able to use der, die, das and ein, eine correctly and make good guesses about a noun's gender.
key_points: All German nouns start with a capital letter.
Every noun has a gender: `der` (masculine), `die` (feminine), `das` (neuter). In the plural it's always `die`.
Indefinite article: `ein` (der/das nouns), `eine` (die nouns); no indefinite article in the plural.
Learn every noun with its article – endings like -ung (die) or -chen (das) help.
Compound nouns take the gender of their last part: `die Haustür`.

sections.heading: Nouns start with a capital letter

blocks.text: In German **every noun** is capitalised – not just names: `der Tisch`, `die Stadt`, `das Haus`, `die Liebe`. This helps you spot the nouns in a sentence.

items.de: Der Hund ist groß.
items.en: The dog is big.

items.de: Die Stadt ist sehr schön.
items.en: The city is very beautiful.

blocks.why: `Auto` is a noun, so it starts with a capital letter.

blocks.text: Every German noun has a grammatical gender: masculine, feminine or neuter. You can see it in the article. In the plural, the definite article is always `die`.
Grammatical gender is not always natural gender: `das Mädchen` (the girl) is neuter, and things can be masculine or feminine: `der Tisch`, `die Tür`.
Learn every noun **with its article** – never just *Tisch*, always `der Tisch`. Many learners use colours: blue for der, red for die, green for das.
Pronouns follow the grammatical gender: `Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist schön.` – here *it* is `er`!

blocks.why: `eine` is only for feminine (die) nouns. Masculine and neuter nouns take `ein`.

blocks.text: Use **ein/eine** when you mention something for the first time or when it's not a specific one (*a* car). Use **der/die/das** when it's already known, specific or the only one (*the* car).

items.de: Das ist ein Haus. Das Haus ist alt.
items.en: That is a house. The house is old.
items.note: first mention → ein; already known → das

items.de: Ich habe eine Frage.
items.en: I have a question.

items.de: Die Sonne scheint.
items.en: The sun is shining.

blocks.why: `ein/eine` has no plural. Just leave the article out, like English *apples*.

blocks.text: There's no perfect rule, but these patterns are very reliable:

head: Pattern
Gender
Examples
rows: die Wohnung, die Gesundheit, die Möglichkeit, die Freundschaft, die Information
das Mädchen, das Brötchen, das Büchlein
der Mann, der Vater, der Lehrer
der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer

blocks.why: Nouns ending in -chen are always neuter – even when they mean a person.

blocks.text: Female persons are usually `die`: `die Frau`, `die Mutter`, `die Lehrerin`. The big exception is `das Mädchen` (because of -chen).
German loves to combine nouns into one long word. The **last** part decides the gender and the main meaning; the first part just describes it.

items.de: das Haus + die Tür → die Haustür
items.en: the front door

items.de: der Kaffee + die Tasse → die Kaffeetasse
items.en: the coffee cup

items.de: die Kinder + das Zimmer → das Kinderzimmer
items.en: the children's room

blocks.why: The last part is `die Tasse`, so the whole word is feminine.

blocks.text: Compounds are written as **one** word with one capital letter: `das Kinderzimmer`, not *das Kinder Zimmer*.

exercises.en: The man is called Peter.
exercises.explain: Male persons are masculine: `der Mann`.

exercises.en: That is a newspaper.
exercises.explain: Nouns ending in -ung are feminine: `die Zeitung` → `eine Zeitung`.

exercises.en: The girl is five years old.
exercises.explain: -chen nouns are always neuter: `das Mädchen`.

exercises.en: The children's room is small.
exercises.explain: The last part decides: `das Zimmer` → `das Kinderzimmer`.

exercises.q: Ich habe ein Auto. ___ Auto ist rot.
exercises.en: I have a car. The car is red.
exercises.explain: The car is already known (second mention), so use the definite article: `das Auto`.

exercises.en: The flat is very nice.
exercises.explain: -ung → feminine: `die Wohnung`.

exercises.en: That is a table.
exercises.explain: `der Tisch` is masculine → `ein Tisch`.

exercises.en: Summer is nice.
exercises.explain: Seasons are masculine: `der Sommer`.

exercises.en: Where is the coffee cup?
exercises.explain: The last part is `die Tasse`, so: `die Kaffeetasse`.

accept: Ein Hund ist das.
exercises.en: That is a dog.
exercises.explain: `der Hund` → indefinite `ein Hund`.

accept: Groß ist die Wohnung.
exercises.en: The flat is big.
exercises.explain: -ung → `die Wohnung`. The verb `ist` is in position 2.

exercises.en: Is the front door open?
exercises.explain: Yes/no question: verb first. `die Tür` → `die Haustür`.

title: Plural der Nomen
summary: You'll be able to form and recognise the plural of common nouns and use them with the article die.
key_points: The plural article is always **die**: der Tisch → die Tische, das Buch → die Bücher.
There are several plural endings: -e, ¨-e, -er/¨-er, -(e)n, -s, or no ending (sometimes only an umlaut).
Most feminine nouns take -(e)n; -s is for words like Auto, Hotel, Handy.
There is no plural of ein/eine: ein Buch → Bücher.
Learn every noun with its article and plural: der Tisch, -e.

sections.heading: One article for all plurals: die

blocks.text: In the singular, German has three articles: der, die, das. In the plural it's easy: the definite article is **always** `die` – whatever the gender of the noun.
A plural noun needs a plural verb, just like `sie` (they): `Das Buch ist neu.` → `Die Bücher sind neu.` And `Das ist …` becomes `Das sind …`.

blocks.why: In the plural the article is always die – even for das and der nouns.

blocks.text: Unfortunately, there is no single plural ending. There are six main patterns. Some of them also add an umlaut to the stem vowel (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü, au → äu).

blocks.caption: The main plural patterns
head: Ending
Examples
Typical nouns
rows: der Tag → die Tag**e**, der Freund → die Freund**e**
der Stuhl → die St**ü**hl**e**, die Stadt → die St**ä**dt**e**
many masculine nouns, some short feminine nouns
das Kind → die Kind**er**, das Buch → die B**ü**ch**er**
many short neuter nouns (also der Mann → die Männer)
die Lampe → die Lampe**n**, die Frau → die Frau**en**
das Auto → die Auto**s**, das Hotel → die Hotel**s**
nouns ending in -a, -i, -o, -u, -y and many international words
der Lehrer → die Lehrer, der Vater → die V**ä**ter
masculine and neuter nouns ending in -er, -el, -en; all nouns ending in -chen

blocks.text: Feminine nouns are the easiest: most take **-n** or **-en**. Nouns ending in -in double the n: `die Lehrerin → die Lehrerinnen`, `die Freundin → die Freundinnen`.

items.de: Ich habe zwei Brüder und eine Schwester.
items.en: I have two brothers and one sister.
items.note: der Bruder → die Brüder (umlaut, no ending)

items.de: Die Kinder spielen im Park.
items.en: The children are playing in the park.

items.de: Die Zimmer sind groß.
items.en: The rooms are big.

items.de: Ich habe zwei Handys.
items.en: I have two mobile phones.

blocks.why: English adds -s to almost every noun. In German, -s is only for certain words (Autos, Hotels, Handys). Nouns ending in -er usually take no ending.

blocks.text: `ein` and `eine` mean *a* / *one*, so they have no plural form. In the plural you simply use the noun on its own – just like English *books*.

items.de: Das ist ein Apfel. – Das sind Äpfel.
items.en: That is an apple. – Those are apples.

items.de: Ich habe ein Kind. – Wir haben drei Kinder.
items.en: I have one child. – We have three children.

blocks.why: There is no plural of ein/eine. Just leave the article out.

sections.heading: Learn the plural with every noun

blocks.text: You can't always predict the plural, so learn each noun as a package: **article + singular + plural**. Dictionaries and word lists use a short notation:
Some nouns exist only in the plural: `die Eltern` (parents), `die Leute` (people). Use them with a plural verb: `Die Leute sind nett.`

exercises.en: The tables are new.
exercises.explain: In the plural the article is always die – also for der nouns like der Tisch.

exercises.en: The child is playing. – The children are playing.
exercises.explain: das Kind → die Kinder: many short neuter nouns take -er. German doesn't use -s here.

exercises.q: Das ist ein Buch. – Das sind ___.
exercises.en: That is a book. – Those are books.
exercises.explain: ein/eine has no plural form. In the plural the noun stands alone: Bücher.

exercises.en: I have two brothers.
exercises.explain: der Bruder → die Brüder: no ending, but an umlaut (u → ü). Bruder without the umlaut is the singular.

exercises.en: The hotels in Berlin are expensive.
exercises.explain: das Hotel → die Hotels: many international words take -s.

exercises.en: The women come from Spain.
exercises.explain: Most feminine nouns take -(e)n: die Frau → die Frauen.

exercises.en: The flat has three rooms.
exercises.explain: Nouns ending in -er often take no plural ending: das Zimmer → die Zimmer.

exercises.en: The books are very good.
exercises.explain: die Bücher is plural (= sie, they), so the verb is plural too: sind.

exercises.en: The apples are red.
exercises.explain: der Apfel → die Äpfel: nouns ending in -el take no ending, but here the vowel gets an umlaut (A → Ä).

accept: Im Park spielen die Kinder.
exercises.en: The children are playing in the park.
exercises.explain: das Kind → die Kinder. A plural subject needs a plural verb: spielen.

accept: Drei Schwestern habe ich.
exercises.en: I have three sisters.
exercises.explain: die Schwester → die Schwestern (-n). With a number there is no article.

accept: Sehr teuer sind die Autos.
exercises.en: The cars are very expensive.
exercises.explain: das Auto → die Autos (-s). The plural subject die Autos takes the plural verb sind.

title: Satzbau: Verb an Position 2
title_en: Word order: the verb in position 2
summary: You'll be able to put the verb in the right place in statements and yes/no questions, and join sentences with und, aber, oder and denn.
key_points: In a statement the conjugated verb is always in **position 2**.
Position 1 can be the subject or something else (heute, am Montag, in Berlin) – then the subject comes right **after** the verb.
In yes/no questions the verb is in **position 1**: Kommst du heute?
und, aber, oder, denn stand at **position 0**: they don't count and don't change the word order.

sections.heading: The golden rule: the verb is in position 2

blocks.text: A German statement is built around the conjugated verb. It always stands in **position 2**. Careful: a position is not the same as a word. `Meine Schwester` or `am Montag` is one position – one block of meaning.
Count the blocks, not the words: `Am Montag` (1) `arbeitet` (2) `Tom` … The verb is always the second block.

sections.heading: Starting with time or place: the subject moves behind the verb

blocks.text: German sentences often start with a time expression (heute, morgen, am Montag, um 8 Uhr) or a place. The verb stays in position 2 – so the subject moves **behind** the verb. This is called *inversion*.

items.de: Am Wochenende spiele ich Fußball.
items.en: At the weekend I play football.

items.de: Um 8 Uhr beginnt der Kurs.
items.en: The course starts at 8 o'clock.
items.note: Um 8 Uhr is one block in position 1

items.de: In Wien wohnt meine Tante.
items.en: My aunt lives in Vienna.

blocks.why: In English the subject comes before the verb (Today I go…). In German the verb must be in position 2, so the subject goes after it.

sections.heading: Yes/no questions: the verb comes first

blocks.text: For a question you can answer with *ja* or *nein*, put the verb in **position 1** and the subject right after it. German has no helper verb like English *do*.

items.de: Sprichst du Englisch? – Ja, ein bisschen.
items.en: Do you speak English? – Yes, a little.

items.de: Arbeitet Paul heute? – Nein, heute hat er frei.
items.en: Is Paul working today? – No, he's off today.
items.note: in the answer: heute (1) hat (2) er

blocks.why: German doesn't use a helper verb like *do* in questions. The main verb itself moves to position 1.

blocks.text: These four words join two main clauses: **und** (and), **aber** (but), **oder** (or), **denn** (because). They stand at **position 0** – outside the clause – so they don't count. After them comes a normal clause with the verb in position 2.
Compare English *but tomorrow I have time*: in German the connector doesn't count, but `morgen` takes position 1 – so the verb comes next and the subject follows: `aber morgen habe ich Zeit`.

blocks.wrong: Ich lerne Deutsch, denn wohne ich in Wien.
blocks.right: Ich lerne Deutsch, denn ich wohne in Wien.
blocks.why: denn is at position 0 and doesn't count. ich is position 1, so the verb wohne comes after it.

blocks.text: Always put a comma before **aber** and **denn**; before **und** and **oder** you usually don't need one. Watch out: **weil** also means *because*, but it sends the verb to the end – you'll learn it later. For now, use **denn**.

exercises.en: Today I'm going to the cinema.
exercises.explain: heute is in position 1, so the verb gehe takes position 2 and the subject ich follows.

accept: Ich arbeite am Wochenende.
exercises.en: I work at the weekend.
exercises.explain: am Wochenende (position 1) – arbeite (position 2) – ich. Or start with the subject: Ich arbeite am Wochenende.

exercises.en: Do you speak German?
exercises.explain: Yes/no questions start with the verb; there is no helper verb like *do*. With du the verb is sprichst (e → i).

exercises.en: Do you have time today?
exercises.explain: In a yes/no question the verb comes first: du hast → Hast du …? (capital letter at the start of the sentence).

accept: Ich gehe heute ins Kino.
Ins Kino gehe ich heute.
exercises.en: I'm going to the cinema today.
exercises.explain: Whatever comes first, the verb gehe is always in position 2.

exercises.en: On Monday Anna is going to Berlin.
exercises.explain: am Montag is position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject Anna follows. Anna = sie → fährt (a → ä).

accept: Wir fahren morgen nach Hamburg.
Nach Hamburg fahren wir morgen.
exercises.en: Tomorrow we're going to Hamburg.
exercises.explain: morgen (1) – fahren (2) – wir. The subject moves behind the verb.

accept: Die Kinder kommen heute Abend.
exercises.en: The children are coming this evening.
exercises.explain: heute Abend is one block in position 1, so the verb kommen is next, then the subject die Kinder.

exercises.q: Ich lerne Deutsch, denn ___ in Wien.
exercises.en: I'm learning German because I live in Vienna.
exercises.explain: denn is at position 0 and doesn't change the word order: ich (1) wohne (2).

exercises.q: Ich bin müde, ___ ich arbeite noch. (but)
exercises.en: I'm tired, but I'm still working.
exercises.explain: aber = but. It stands at position 0, so the clause after it has normal word order: ich arbeite.

exercises.en: Do you live in Berlin?
exercises.explain: In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then the subject. (Du wohnst in Berlin? with rising intonation is also possible in speech.)

exercises.answer: Ich trinke Kaffee und du trinkst Tee.
accept: Ich trinke Kaffee und Tee trinkst du.
Kaffee trinke ich und du trinkst Tee.
Kaffee trinke ich und Tee trinkst du.
Du trinkst Tee und ich trinke Kaffee.
Du trinkst Tee und Kaffee trinke ich.
Tee trinkst du und ich trinke Kaffee.
Tee trinkst du und Kaffee trinke ich.
exercises.en: I drink coffee and you drink tea.
exercises.explain: und is at position 0. Both clauses have the verb in position 2: ich trinke …, du trinkst …

title: W-Fragen
summary: You'll be able to ask for information with question words like wer, wo, wann and warum – and understand the typical answers.
key_points: W-questions start with a question word in position 1; the verb follows in position 2, then the subject.
wo = where (place), woher = where from, wohin = where to.
wie viel + singular (Zeit, Geld), wie viele + plural (Kinder, Bücher).
welcher, welche, welches have the same endings as der, die, das.
No helper verb like *do*: Where do you live? → Wo wohnst du?

blocks.text: Questions that ask for information start with a question word. Almost all of them begin with *w*, so they're called W-questions. The rule from the last chapter still applies: the verb is in **position 2**, and the subject comes right after it.

items.de: Was machst du am Wochenende? – Ich spiele Tennis.
items.en: What are you doing at the weekend? – I'm playing tennis.

items.de: Wann beginnt der Film? – Um 20 Uhr.
items.en: When does the film start? – At 8 pm.

items.de: Warum lernst du Deutsch? – Ich wohne in Wien.
items.en: Why are you learning German? – I live in Vienna.

blocks.why: The verb must come directly after the question word (position 2), before the subject.

blocks.text: Match question and answer: **wo?** → `in` Berlin, **woher?** → `aus` Berlin, **wohin?** → `nach` Berlin. And to ask for a name, say `Wie heißt du?` or `Wie ist Ihr Name?` – with **wie**, not was.

blocks.why: False friend: German **wer** means *who*, not *where*. *Where* is **wo**.
To ask where someone comes from, use **woher** (where from). **wo** only asks where something or someone is.

sections.heading: How much, how many, how old

blocks.text: **wie** combines with other words: `wie viel` (how much), `wie viele` (how many), `wie alt` (how old), `wie spät` (what time). Use **wie viel** with singular nouns you can't count (Zeit, Geld, Wasser) and **wie viele** with plural nouns.

items.de: Wie viel kostet die Jacke? – 50 Euro.
items.en: How much is the jacket? – 50 euros.
items.note: Was kostet die Jacke? is also very common.

items.de: Wie viele Brüder hast du? – Zwei.
items.en: How many brothers do you have? – Two.

blocks.text: **welch-** means *which*. It takes the same ending as the definite article: der → welch**er**, die → welch**e**, das → welch**es**, plural die → welch**e**.
Look at the last letter of the article: de**r** → welche**r**, di**e** → welch**e**, da**s** → welche**s**.

exercises.en: Where do you live? – In Hamburg.
exercises.explain: The answer is a place (in Hamburg), so you ask with wo (where).

exercises.en: Where are you from? – From Austria.
exercises.explain: The answer starts with aus (from), so the question word is woher (where from).

exercises.q: ___ heißt du? – Ich heiße Lena. (question word)
exercises.en: What's your name? – My name is Lena.
exercises.explain: German asks for a name with wie: Wie heißt du? (literally: How are you called?)

exercises.q: ___ ist das? – Das ist mein Bruder.
exercises.en: Who is that? – That's my brother.
exercises.explain: You ask about a person, so use wer (who). Careful: wer is not *where*.

exercises.en: When does the course start? – At 9 o'clock.
exercises.explain: The verb comes in position 2 after the question word. der Kurs = er → beginnt.

exercises.en: Where are you from?
exercises.explain: Question word (1) – verb (2) – subject: Woher kommt ihr?

exercises.en: Where are you going? – To Berlin.
exercises.explain: ihr fahrt – there is no vowel change with ihr (only with du and er/sie/es).

exercises.en: How many children do you have? – Two.
exercises.explain: Kinder is plural, so you use wie viele (how many).

exercises.q: ___ Zeit hast du? – Eine Stunde. (how much)
exercises.en: How much time do you have? – One hour.
exercises.explain: Zeit is singular and uncountable, so you use wie viel (two words).

exercises.en: What are you doing at the weekend?
exercises.explain: was (1) – machst (2) – du – am Wochenende.

exercises.q: ___ Buch ist gut? – Das Buch hier.
exercises.en: Which book is good? – This book here.
exercises.explain: das Buch → welches: welch- takes the -s of das.

exercises.answer: Wann fährt der Zug nach München?
exercises.en: When does the train to Munich leave?
exercises.explain: wann (1) – fährt (2) – der Zug (subject) – nach München.

title: Negation mit „nicht“ und „kein“
summary: You'll be able to make sentences negative with nicht and kein – and answer negative questions with doch.
key_points: Use **kein** for nouns with ein/eine or with no article: ein Auto → kein Auto, Zeit → keine Zeit.
kein has the same endings as ein: kein (der/das), keine (die and plural); masculine after verbs like haben: keinen.
Use **nicht** for everything else: verbs, adjectives, names, places, nouns with der/die/das or mein.
nicht often goes at the end, but before adjectives, places and phrases with a preposition.
To say *yes* to a negative question, answer **doch**.

blocks.text: **kein** means *no*, *not a* or *not any*. Use it when the positive sentence has **ein/eine** or **no article** in front of the noun. It has the same endings as ein.
After verbs like haben, trinken or kaufen, a masculine noun takes **keinen** (just like einen): `Ich habe keinen Bruder.` `Er trinkt keinen Kaffee.` You'll learn why in the chapter on the accusative.

items.de: Wir haben keine Kinder.
items.en: We don't have any children.

items.de: Heute habe ich keine Zeit.
items.en: I don't have time today.

items.de: Er trinkt keinen Kaffee.
items.en: He doesn't drink coffee.

blocks.why: Zeit has no article, so you negate it with kein – not with nicht.
nicht + ein becomes kein.

blocks.text: Use **nicht** for everything that is not a noun with ein or without an article: verbs, adjectives, names, places, and nouns with der/die/das or mein/dein.

head: What you negate
Example
rows: Das ist **nicht** der Bus nach Berlin.

blocks.why: kein only goes with ordinary nouns like Auto, Zeit or Bücher. Names are negated with nicht.

blocks.text: The verb stays in position 2 – nicht never changes that. For the position of nicht, these basic rules work in most A1 sentences:

head: Rule
Example
rows: whole sentence negated → nicht at the **end**
**before** places and phrases with a preposition

items.de: Ich verstehe das nicht.
items.en: I don't understand that.

items.de: Er kommt nicht aus Spanien.
items.en: He doesn't come from Spain.

items.de: Ich koche nicht gern.
items.en: I don't like cooking.

blocks.why: English puts *not* before the main verb (I don't come). In German the verb stays in position 2, and nicht goes to the end here.

blocks.text: You answer a normal question with **ja** or **nein**. But if the question is **negative** (with nicht or kein) and you want to say *yes*, use **doch**. It contradicts the negative question.
Think of **doch** as an emphatic *Yes, I do! / Yes, I am!* – said when the other person expects a *no*.

blocks.wrong: Bist du nicht müde? – Ja, ich bin müde.
blocks.right: Bist du nicht müde? – Doch, ich bin müde.
blocks.why: The question is negative and you contradict it, so the answer is doch, not ja.

exercises.q: Das ist ___ Hund. Das ist eine Katze.
exercises.en: That's not a dog. That's a cat.
exercises.explain: ein Hund → kein Hund. der Hund is masculine, so no ending: kein.

exercises.en: I have no time.
exercises.explain: die Zeit is feminine and has no article here, so it's keine Zeit.

exercises.en: I don't live in Berlin.
exercises.explain: You negate a place (in Berlin), not a noun with ein – so use nicht, before the preposition.

exercises.en: We don't have any children.
exercises.explain: Kinder is plural without an article, so you use kein – in the plural: keine.

exercises.q: Das ist ___ Tisch, das ist ein Stuhl. (kein)
exercises.en: That's not a table, that's a chair.
exercises.explain: ein Tisch → kein Tisch (masculine, no ending after Das ist).

accept: Heute komme ich nicht.
exercises.en: I'm not coming today.
exercises.explain: The whole sentence is negated, so nicht goes to the end. The verb komme stays in position 2.

exercises.q: Das Wetter ist ___ gut. (nicht or kein?)
exercises.en: The weather isn't good.
exercises.explain: gut is an adjective. Adjectives are negated with nicht, which goes before them.

exercises.q: Das ist ___ Anna. Das ist Maria.
exercises.en: That isn't Anna. That's Maria.
exercises.explain: Names are negated with nicht, never with kein.

accept: Nach Hamburg fahren wir nicht.
exercises.en: We're not going to Hamburg.
exercises.explain: nicht comes before a place with a preposition: nicht nach Hamburg.

exercises.q: Er trinkt ___ Kaffee. (kein → der Kaffee, Akkusativ)
exercises.en: He doesn't drink coffee.
exercises.explain: der Kaffee is masculine. After trinken it takes the accusative, like einen: keinen Kaffee.

exercises.q: Hast du keine Zeit? – ___, ich habe Zeit.
exercises.en: Don't you have time? – Yes, I do have time.
exercises.explain: The question is negative (keine Zeit) and the answer contradicts it, so you say doch.

accept: Er spricht Deutsch nicht gut.
Deutsch spricht er nicht gut.
exercises.en: He doesn't speak German well.
exercises.explain: nicht goes directly before gut. The verb spricht stays in position 2.

title: Der Akkusativ
summary: You'll be able to say what or whom someone has, needs, buys or sees, using the correct accusative articles and pronouns.
key_points: The direct object (the person or thing the action is done to) is in the accusative.
Only masculine nouns change: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen.
Feminine, neuter and plural look exactly like the nominative.
haben, brauchen, kaufen, suchen, sehen, möchten and es gibt are followed by the accusative.
Accusative pronouns: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie/Sie. für and ohne always take the accusative.

blocks.text: In `Der Mann kauft den Apfel`, **der Mann** is the subject: he does the action. The subject is in the **nominative**. **den Apfel** is the direct object: the thing that is bought. The direct object is in the **accusative**.
Quick test: ask **Wer?** (who?) to find the subject and **Wen?** (whom?) or **Was?** (what?) to find the direct object.

items.de: Ich kaufe einen Tisch.
items.en: I'm buying a table.

items.de: Anna sucht den Bahnhof.
items.en: Anna is looking for the station.

blocks.text: German word order is flexible, but the article shows who does what: `Den Kaffee trinkt Peter.` still means *Peter drinks the coffee*, because `den` marks the object.

items.de: Ich habe einen Bruder.
items.en: I have a brother.

items.de: Ich brauche eine Tasche.
items.en: I need a bag.

items.de: Wir kaufen ein Auto.
items.en: We are buying a car.

items.de: Sie hat keine Kinder.
items.en: She has no children.

blocks.text: Only the masculine gets an extra **-n** in the accusative: `den`, `einen`, `keinen`. Everything else stays the same.

blocks.why: Bruder is masculine (der Bruder). As the object of haben it is accusative, so ein becomes einen.

blocks.text: Most verbs that have a direct object use the accusative. Very common ones: `haben`, `brauchen`, `kaufen`, `suchen`, `sehen`, `möchten`, `essen`, `trinken`, `nehmen`. The expression `es gibt` (there is / there are) is always followed by the accusative too.

items.de: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
items.en: I'd like a coffee, please.

items.de: Siehst du den Bus?
items.en: Do you see the bus?

items.de: Hier gibt es einen Park.
items.en: There is a park here.

blocks.why: After es gibt the noun is accusative: der Supermarkt → einen Supermarkt.
sein is not an action done to something. After sein you use the nominative, never the accusative.

items.de: Ich liebe dich.
items.en: I love you.

items.de: Wir besuchen euch morgen.
items.en: We'll visit you tomorrow.

items.de: Der Kaffee ist gut. Ich trinke ihn gern.
items.en: The coffee is good. I like drinking it.
items.note: der Kaffee → ihn, even though it's a thing

blocks.wrong: Der Pullover ist schön. Ich kaufe es.
blocks.right: Der Pullover ist schön. Ich kaufe ihn.
blocks.why: The pronoun follows the gender of the noun: der Pullover is masculine → ihn, even for things.

blocks.text: The prepositions `für` (for) and `ohne` (without) are always followed by the accusative.

items.de: Das Geschenk ist für dich.
items.en: The present is for you.

items.de: Das Buch ist für den Lehrer.
items.en: The book is for the teacher.

items.de: Ich trinke Tee ohne Zucker.
items.en: I drink tea without sugar.

blocks.text: Learn them as a pair: **für** and **ohne** + accusative, e.g. `für mich`, `ohne ihn`.

exercises.en: I have a dog.
exercises.explain: der Hund is masculine and the object of haben → accusative einen.

exercises.en: We are buying a lamp.
exercises.explain: die Lampe is feminine. Feminine doesn't change in the accusative: eine.

exercises.en: I need a computer.
exercises.explain: Masculine accusative: ein → einen.

exercises.en: Do you see the station?
exercises.explain: der Bahnhof is the object of sehen → accusative den.

exercises.q: Hier gibt es ___ Supermarkt. (kein, der Supermarkt)
exercises.en: There is no supermarket here.
exercises.explain: es gibt takes the accusative: masculine kein → keinen.

exercises.en: That is a table.
exercises.explain: After sein you use the nominative: ein Tisch.

exercises.q: Der Kaffee ist kalt. Ich trinke ___ nicht.
exercises.en: The coffee is cold. I'm not drinking it.
exercises.explain: der Kaffee is masculine and the object → accusative pronoun ihn.

exercises.en: I love you.
exercises.explain: du in the accusative is dich.

exercises.en: The flowers are for us.
exercises.explain: für takes the accusative: wir → uns.

accept: Einen Pullover kaufe ich.
exercises.en: I'm buying a pullover.
exercises.explain: The verb is in position 2; der Pullover becomes einen Pullover in the accusative.

accept: Es gibt hier keinen Park.
Es gibt keinen Park hier.
Keinen Park gibt es hier.
exercises.en: There is no park here.
exercises.explain: gibt is in position 2. es gibt + accusative: kein → keinen (der Park).

exercises.answer: Ich kaufe den Kuchen für sie.
accept: Ich kaufe für sie den Kuchen.
Den Kuchen kaufe ich für sie.
Für sie kaufe ich den Kuchen.
exercises.en: I'm buying the cake for her.
exercises.explain: der Kuchen → den Kuchen (object of kaufen); für + accusative pronoun sie.

title: Possessivartikel
summary: You'll be able to talk about your family and your things with mein, dein, sein, ihr and the others, with the right endings.
key_points: Each person has its own possessive: mein, dein, sein, ihr, sein, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr.
Possessives take the same endings as ein and kein.
Feminine and plural: meine. Masculine accusative: meinen.
sein or ihr? That depends on the owner, not on the thing owned.

items.de: Das ist mein Bruder.
items.en: This is my brother.

items.de: Wie ist Ihr Name?
items.en: What is your name? (formal)

items.de: Das ist unser Haus.
items.en: This is our house.

blocks.text: `Ihr` with a capital I means *your* (formal), just like `Sie`. Lowercase `ihr` means *her* or *their*.

sections.heading: Endings: just like ein and kein

blocks.text: Possessive articles take the same endings as `ein` and `kein`. So you add **-e** for feminine and plural, and **-en** for masculine in the accusative.

blocks.caption: mein (the same pattern for dein, sein, ihr, unser, Ihr)
head: maskulin
feminin
neutral
Plural

items.de: Meine Mutter heißt Eva.
items.en: My mother is called Eva.

items.de: Mein Auto ist alt.
items.en: My car is old.

items.de: Meine Kinder sind fünf und acht.
items.en: My children are five and eight.

items.de: Ich suche meinen Schlüssel.
items.en: I'm looking for my key.

blocks.why: die Schwester is feminine, so you need the ending -e: meine.
der Schlüssel is masculine and the object of suchen → accusative meinen.

blocks.text: The **owner** decides between `sein` and `ihr`: a man or a masculine/neuter noun → `sein`; a woman or several people → `ihr`. The **thing owned** decides the ending.

items.de: Peter besucht seine Mutter.
items.en: Peter visits his mother.

items.de: Anna besucht ihren Vater.
items.en: Anna visits her father.
items.note: owner Anna → ihr; der Vater, accusative → -en

items.de: Paul und Lisa suchen ihre Katze.
items.en: Paul and Lisa are looking for their cat.

blocks.why: Anna is the owner, and she is female → ihr. The dog (der Hund) only decides the ending -en.

blocks.text: Ask two questions. 1) Who is the owner? → `sein`, `ihr`, ... 2) What gender and case is the thing? → the ending.
`unser` simply adds the endings: `unsere`, `unseren`. `euer` usually drops its second **e** when an ending is added: `eure`, `euren`.

items.de: Wir besuchen unseren Opa.
items.en: We are visiting our grandpa.

items.de: Wo ist eure Wohnung?
items.en: Where is your flat?

exercises.en: This is my mother.
exercises.explain: die Mutter is feminine → meine.

exercises.en: What is your name, please? (formal)
exercises.explain: Formal your = Ihr with a capital I. Lowercase ihr means her or their.

exercises.en: I'm looking for my key.
exercises.explain: der Schlüssel is masculine and the object of suchen → meinen.

exercises.en: Peter visits his sister.
exercises.explain: The owner is Peter → sein. die Schwester is feminine → seine.

exercises.en: Lisa, where do your parents live?
exercises.explain: Eltern is plural → deine.

exercises.en: Anna is looking for her dog.
exercises.explain: The owner is Anna → ihr. der Hund is masculine accusative → ihren.

exercises.en: We are selling our car.
exercises.explain: das Auto is neuter: no ending in the accusative, just like ein Auto.

exercises.en: Kids, where are your books?
exercises.explain: Talking to several children → euer. Bücher is plural → eure.

exercises.en: Mr Braun, is this your bag?
exercises.explain: Formal your = Ihr. die Tasche is feminine → Ihre.

accept: Mein Bruder ist das.
exercises.en: This is my brother.
exercises.explain: der Bruder is masculine nominative → mein, no ending.

accept: Meinen Schlüssel finde ich nicht.
exercises.en: I can't find my key.
exercises.explain: Verb in position 2, nicht at the end. der Schlüssel is the object → meinen.

accept: Heute besuchen wir unsere Oma.
Wir besuchen unsere Oma heute.
Unsere Oma besuchen wir heute.
exercises.en: We are visiting our grandma today.
exercises.explain: die Oma is feminine → unsere. The verb stays in position 2.

title: Modalverben
summary: You'll be able to say what you can, must, want, would like, may and should do, with the infinitive in the right place.
key_points: können (can), müssen (must, have to), wollen (want), möchten (would like), dürfen (may, be allowed to), sollen (should, be supposed to).
ich and er/sie/es have the same form, without an ending: ich kann, er kann.
Sentence bracket: the modal verb is in position 2, the infinitive goes to the very end.
möchte is polite, will is direct.
muss nicht = don't have to; darf nicht = must not.

sections.heading: Six modal verbs and their meanings

blocks.text: Modal verbs say *how* you relate to an action: is it possible, necessary, wanted, allowed? They usually come with a second verb in the infinitive.
In the singular, most modal verbs change their vowel (können → `kann`, müssen → `muss`, wollen → `will`, dürfen → `darf`). And ich and er/sie/es are identical, with no ending: `ich kann`, `er kann`.

blocks.why: Modal verbs have no -t for er/sie/es: er kann, sie muss, es darf.

blocks.text: The modal verb is conjugated and stands in **position 2** (or position 1 in yes/no questions). The second verb is an **infinitive** and goes to the **very end**. Together they form a bracket around the rest of the sentence.

items.de: Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
items.en: I can't come today.

items.de: Wir müssen morgen arbeiten.
items.en: We have to work tomorrow.

items.de: Kannst du gut schwimmen?
items.en: Can you swim well?

items.de: Was möchtest du essen?
items.en: What would you like to eat?

blocks.why: The infinitive always goes to the very end of the sentence.
After a modal verb there is no zu (unlike English have to / want to).

blocks.text: `wollen` is direct and strong: *I want*. `möchte` is polite: *I would like*. In a shop, a café or with people you don't know, use `möchte`. `möchte` can also stand alone with an object.

items.de: Ich möchte bitte ein Wasser.
items.en: I'd like a water, please.

items.de: Das Kind will ein Eis!
items.en: The child wants an ice cream!

blocks.text: Ordering food? Always `Ich möchte ...`. `Ich will ...` sounds like a demanding child.
`nicht müssen` means it is **not necessary**. `nicht dürfen` means it is **not allowed**.

items.de: Morgen ist Sonntag. Ich muss nicht arbeiten.
items.en: Tomorrow is Sunday. I don't have to work.

items.de: Du darfst hier nicht parken.
items.en: You're not allowed to park here.

blocks.text: Careful, false friend: English *must not* = German **darf nicht**. German **muss nicht** = *don't have to*.

exercises.en: I can swim well.
exercises.explain: ich kann: no ending for ich.

exercises.en: You have to work today.

exercises.en: May I park here?
exercises.explain: ich darf: same as er/sie/es, no ending. In a yes/no question the modal verb comes first.

exercises.en: What would you like to drink?
exercises.explain: ihr möchtet: the ihr form ends in -t.

exercises.q: Im Café: Ich ___ bitte einen Tee.
exercises.en: At the café: I'd like a tea, please.
exercises.explain: möchte is the polite way to order. will sounds rude.

exercises.en: You should drink more water.

exercises.en: Tomorrow is Sunday. I don't have to work.

exercises.explain: Not allowed = nicht dürfen. ihr dürft keeps the ü in the plural.

exercises.en: I can't come today.
exercises.explain: Modal verb in position 2, infinitive kommen at the very end, nicht right before it.

title: Trennbare Verben
summary: You'll be able to talk about your daily routine with separable verbs like aufstehen, einkaufen and anrufen, putting the prefix in the right place.
key_points: Many verbs have a separable prefix: auf|stehen, ein|kaufen, an|rufen, fern|sehen ...
In a main clause the verb is in position 2 and the prefix goes to the very end.
The stress is on the prefix: AUFstehen, EINkaufen.
With a modal verb the verb stays together at the end: Ich muss früh aufstehen.
be-, ver-, er- and ent- never separate: bezahlen, verstehen.

blocks.text: Some verbs consist of a **prefix** + a verb, e.g. `auf` + `stehen` = `aufstehen` (to get up). In a normal sentence the two parts split up. Here are the most important ones:
The stress is always on the separable prefix: **AUF**stehen, **EIN**kaufen, **AN**rufen. If you hear the stress at the start, the verb probably separates.

sections.heading: The prefix goes to the end

blocks.text: The conjugated verb stands in **position 2** (or position 1 in yes/no questions), and the prefix goes to the **very end** of the sentence. This forms a bracket, just like with modal verbs. Vowel changes stay: `fernsehen` → `er sieht fern`, `einladen` → `du lädst ein`, `er lädt ein`.

items.de: Ich stehe jeden Tag um 7 Uhr auf.
items.en: I get up at 7 every day.

items.de: Wann kommt der Zug an?
items.en: When does the train arrive?

items.de: Rufst du mich heute an?
items.en: Will you call me today?

items.de: Er lädt seine Freunde ein.
items.en: He invites his friends.

blocks.why: In a main clause the verb splits: the verb in position 2, the prefix at the end.
The prefix goes to the very end of the sentence, after everything else.

sections.heading: With modal verbs: together at the end

blocks.text: When there is a modal verb, the modal verb takes position 2 and the separable verb goes to the end as **one word** in the infinitive.

items.de: Ich muss morgen früh aufstehen.
items.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

items.de: Kannst du mich abholen?
items.en: Can you pick me up?

items.de: Willst du mitkommen?
items.en: Do you want to come along?

blocks.why: With a modal verb the separable verb is an infinitive at the end, written as one word.

sections.heading: Prefixes that never separate: be-, ver-, er-, ent-

blocks.text: Verbs with **be-**, **ver-**, **er-** or **ent-** are inseparable. The prefix always stays on the verb, and it is not stressed: be**ZAH**len, ver**STE**hen.

items.de: Ich bezahle den Kaffee.
items.en: I'm paying for the coffee.

items.de: Verstehst du das?
items.en: Do you understand that?

items.de: Wir besuchen morgen unsere Oma.
items.en: We're visiting our grandma tomorrow.

blocks.why: be- is an inseparable prefix. It never moves to the end.

blocks.text: be-, ver-, er- and ent- are not words on their own, so they stick to the verb. Separable prefixes like `auf`, `an`, `mit`, `ab` are small words that can stand alone.

exercises.explain: fernsehen keeps the vowel change of sehen: er sieht ... fern.

exercises.en: I'll call you tomorrow.
exercises.explain: anrufen: the prefix an goes to the very end.

exercises.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.
exercises.explain: With a modal verb the separable verb stays together as an infinitive at the end.

exercises.en: Will you pick me up at 8?
exercises.explain: abholen: holst du ... ab? In a yes/no question the verb comes first.

exercises.en: I'm paying for the coffee.
exercises.explain: be- is inseparable: ich bezahle.

exercises.en: He invites his friends.
exercises.explain: einladen has a vowel change: er lädt ... ein.

exercises.en: Are you coming along today?
exercises.explain: Yes/no question: verb first, prefix mit at the very end.

exercises.answer: Ich räume heute mein Zimmer auf.
accept: Heute räume ich mein Zimmer auf.
Ich räume mein Zimmer heute auf.
Mein Zimmer räume ich heute auf.
exercises.en: I'm tidying up my room today.
exercises.explain: räume in position 2, the prefix auf at the very end.

accept: Am Samstag müssen wir einkaufen.
Einkaufen müssen wir am Samstag.
exercises.en: We have to go shopping on Saturday.
exercises.explain: Modal verb in position 2, einkaufen together at the end.

title: Der Imperativ
summary: You'll be able to give instructions and make requests to a friend, to a group and to people you say Sie to — and sound polite while doing it.
key_points: Sie-form: infinitive + Sie, verb first: `Kommen Sie bitte!`
du-form: present-tense du-form without du and without -st: du kommst → `Komm!` The e → i change stays (`Nimm!`, `Lies!`), but a → ä does not (`Fahr!`).
ihr-form: present-tense ihr-form without ihr: `Kommt!`
sein is irregular: `Sei!` – `Seid!` – `Seien Sie!`
Separable prefixes go to the end (`Ruf mich an!`); `bitte` and `mal` make a command sound polite and friendly.

sections.heading: Three forms for three kinds of 'you'

blocks.text: German has three words for *you* (`du`, `ihr`, `Sie`), so it also has three imperative forms. The verb always comes **first**. In the du- and ihr-forms the pronoun disappears, but **Sie always stays**.

**Sie-form:** infinitive + `Sie` — it looks like a yes/no question, but you say it like a request and write `!` or `.` at the end. **ihr-form:** the normal present-tense form without `ihr`: ihr kommt → `Kommt!`

items.de: Kommen Sie bitte!
items.en: Please come.

items.de: Kinder, kommt bitte!
items.en: Children, please come.

items.de: Lisa, komm bitte!
items.en: Lisa, please come.

blocks.why: In the formal imperative, Sie is never dropped.

blocks.text: Start with the present-tense du-form, then drop `du` and the ending `-st`: du kommst → `Komm!`, du kaufst → `Kauf!`. If the stem ends in -t or -d, keep an -e: du arbeitest → `Arbeite!`, du wartest → `Warte!`.

blocks.caption: Vowel change: e → i/ie stays, a → ä disappears
head: Infinitive
Present (du)
Imperative (du)

blocks.text: You sometimes see an extra -e (`Komme!`, `Mache!`). It is correct but sounds formal or old-fashioned — in everyday German just say `Komm!`, `Mach!`. Verbs with e → i never take this -e: `Nimm!`, never *Nimme!*

blocks.why: The e → i change of the du-form stays in the imperative: du nimmst → Nimm!
The a → ä change does NOT stay: du fährst, but Fahr!
The du-imperative has no -st ending and no du.

items.de: Sei nicht traurig!
items.en: Don't be sad.

items.de: Seid bitte leise, das Baby schläft.
items.en: Please be quiet, the baby is sleeping.

blocks.text: `Seid!` looks exactly like the present form *ihr seid* — only the pronoun is gone. The Sie-form is `Seien Sie!`, not *Sind Sie!*
The imperative verb is in **position 1**. With separable verbs (chapter 12) the prefix goes to the **end** of the sentence, just like in a normal statement.

items.de: Ruf mich an!
items.en: Call me.

items.de: Steh bitte auf!
items.en: Please get up.

items.de: Macht bitte das Fenster zu!
items.en: Please close the window. (to several people)

items.de: Kaufen Sie bitte Milch ein!
items.en: Please buy some milk.

blocks.why: The prefix separates from the verb and goes to the end.

blocks.text: A bare imperative can sound bossy. Soften it with **bitte** (please) and **mal**, a small word that makes a request sound casual and friendly. `bitte` usually comes right after the verb (or after `Sie`), but it can also stand at the beginning. `mal` comes after the verb, pronoun or `bitte`.

items.de: Warten Sie bitte einen Moment.
items.en: Please wait a moment.

items.de: Bitte hilf mir!
items.en: Please help me!

items.de: Komm mal her!
items.en: Come here (for a moment).

items.de: Sag mal, wo wohnst du?
items.en: Tell me, where do you live?
items.note: Sag mal … is a very common way to start a question.

items.de: Gib mir bitte mal das Salz.
items.en: Could you pass me the salt, please?

blocks.text: Use the Sie-form with strangers, in shops and at work. Use du with friends, family and children, and ihr with a group of them.

exercises.en: Please speak slowly.
exercises.explain: With Sie, use the infinitive + Sie: Sprechen Sie!

exercises.en: Tim, please drink the water.
exercises.explain: du-form imperative: du trinkst → drop du and -st → Trink!

exercises.en: Children, please be quiet.
exercises.explain: Several people you say du to → ihr-form of sein: Seid!

exercises.en: Paul, read the book.
exercises.explain: du liest → Lies! The vowel change e → ie stays in the imperative.

exercises.en: Don't drive so fast, Lisa.
exercises.explain: du fährst, but the a → ä change disappears in the imperative: Fahr! (Fahrt is the ihr-form — Lisa is one person.)

exercises.en: Please wait here.
exercises.explain: Sie-form: infinitive + Sie: Warten Sie!

exercises.en: Max, please take an apple.
exercises.explain: du nimmst → Nimm! The e → i change stays.

exercises.en: Children, please open the window.
exercises.explain: ihr-form: ihr macht auf → Macht … auf! The prefix auf goes to the end.

exercises.en: Ms Klein, please be on time.
exercises.explain: The Sie-form of sein is irregular: Seien Sie!

accept: Bitte ruf mich an!
exercises.en: Please call me.
exercises.explain: The verb ruf is in position 1, the prefix an goes to the end.

accept: Bitte stehen Sie auf!
exercises.en: Please stand up.
exercises.explain: Sie-form: Stehen Sie … auf! — bitte comes after Sie (or at the beginning).

accept: Mach das Fenster mal auf!
exercises.en: Open the window, would you?
exercises.explain: Verb first, prefix auf at the end; mal makes the request sound friendly.

title: Uhrzeit und Zeitangaben
title_en: Telling the time and talking about when
summary: You'll be able to ask and tell the time, both officially and in everyday speech, and say when something happens with um, am, im, von … bis and ab.
key_points: Wie spät ist es? / Wie viel Uhr ist es? asks for the time; Wann? asks when something happens → Um acht Uhr.
Official time uses 24 hours: 19:30 = neunzehn Uhr dreißig.
Informal time: halb points to the NEXT hour — halb acht = 7:30! Also Viertel nach / Viertel vor, fünf nach, zehn vor.
um + clock time; am + days and parts of the day (but in der Nacht); im + months and seasons.
von … bis = from … to; ab = from … on.

blocks.text: To ask what time it is now, say **Wie spät ist es?** or **Wie viel Uhr ist es?** The answer starts with `Es ist …`. To ask when something happens, use **Wann?** — the answer usually starts with `um`.

items.de: Wie spät ist es? – Es ist drei Uhr.
items.en: What time is it? – It's three o'clock.

items.de: Wann beginnt der Kurs? – Um neun Uhr.
items.en: When does the course start? – At nine o'clock.

items.de: Um wie viel Uhr kommst du?
items.en: What time are you coming?

blocks.why: Wann asks when something happens. For the current time, ask Wie spät ist es? or Wie viel Uhr ist es?

blocks.text: On the radio, at the train station, in timetables and opening hours, Germans use the **24-hour clock**: hour + `Uhr` + minutes.
1:00 is `ein Uhr` (not *eins Uhr*) — but without Uhr you say `Es ist eins.` And careful: `Uhr` is the time on the clock, `Stunde` is a period of 60 minutes: Der Film dauert zwei **Stunden**.

In everyday conversation people use the 12-hour clock with **nach** (past), **vor** (to), **Viertel** (quarter) and **halb** (half). The big surprise: `halb` points to the **next** hour. `halb acht` means 'half way to eight' = **7:30**.

blocks.why: halb always counts towards the next hour: halb acht = half an hour before eight.

blocks.text: In the evening, 19:30 is also simply `halb acht` informally. If you need to be clear, add `morgens` or `abends`: um halb acht abends.

sections.heading: Days, months, seasons and parts of the day

blocks.text: All days, months and seasons are masculine (**der**). Days: Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag, Sonntag. Months: Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni, Juli, August, September, Oktober, November, Dezember. Seasons: der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter.
With heute, morgen and gestern you need no preposition: `heute Abend`, `gestern Nachmittag`, `morgen früh` (tomorrow morning). Careful: `morgen` = tomorrow, `der Morgen` = the morning.

sections.heading: Prepositions of time: um, am, im, von … bis, ab

head: Preposition
Used with
Example
rows: um acht Uhr, um halb neun
days, parts of the day, the weekend
am Montag, am Abend, am Wochenende

items.de: Der Film beginnt um acht Uhr.
items.en: The film starts at eight o'clock.

items.de: Am Sonntag arbeite ich nicht.
items.en: I don't work on Sunday.

items.de: Mein Geburtstag ist im Mai.
items.en: My birthday is in May.

items.de: Ich arbeite von Montag bis Freitag.
items.en: I work from Monday to Friday.

items.de: Ab Montag habe ich Urlaub.
items.en: I'm on holiday from Monday.

blocks.why: Days take am; im is for months and seasons.
Nacht is the exception: in der Nacht, not am Nacht.
Clock times need um.

exercises.explain: Clock times take um.

exercises.en: I have Monday off.
exercises.explain: Days of the week take am.

exercises.en: It's half past seven.
exercises.explain: halb points to the next hour: halb acht = 7:30.

exercises.q: ___ ist es? – Es ist zehn nach drei.
exercises.en: What time is it? – It's ten past three.
exercises.explain: To ask the time now, say Wie spät ist es? Wann asks when something happens.

exercises.en: My mother works at night.
exercises.explain: Parts of the day take am — except die Nacht: in der Nacht.

exercises.en: It's quarter past nine.
exercises.explain: 9:15 is a quarter after nine: Viertel nach neun.

exercises.en: We're going on holiday in August.
exercises.explain: Months take im (in + dem).

exercises.q: Das Geschäft ist von 9 ___ 18 Uhr offen. (from … to)
exercises.en: The shop is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.
exercises.explain: from … to = von … bis.

exercises.en: It's twenty to five.
exercises.explain: 16:40 is twenty minutes before five: zwanzig vor fünf.

exercises.answer: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
accept: Um sieben Uhr stehe ich auf.
exercises.en: I get up at seven o'clock.
exercises.explain: um + clock time; the verb is in position 2 and the prefix auf goes to the end.

exercises.answer: Von Montag bis Freitag arbeite ich.
accept: Ich arbeite von Montag bis Freitag.
exercises.en: I work from Monday to Friday.
exercises.explain: If the time phrase von Montag bis Freitag comes first, the verb stays in position 2 and ich follows it.

accept: Ich schlafe am Samstag lange.
Lange schlafe ich am Samstag.
exercises.en: On Saturday I sleep in.
exercises.explain: am + day; the verb schlafe is always in position 2.

title: Präpositionen mit Dativ
summary: You'll be able to use mit, bei, zu, aus, von, nach and seit with the right dative article, and say where you are with im, am and zu Hause.
key_points: mit, bei, zu, aus, von, nach and seit are always followed by the dative.
Dative articles: dem (m), der (f), dem (n), den + -n (plural); einem, einer, einem.
Short forms: zum, zur, beim, vom — and im, am.
Wo? + in/an → dative: im Supermarkt, in der Schule, am Bahnhof.
nach Hause = (going) home; zu Hause = at home.

blocks.text: After certain prepositions, nouns are in the **dative** case. The articles change like this:

In the dative plural the noun itself also gets **-n**: die Kinder → mit den Kinder**n**, die Freunde → mit meinen Freunde**n**. No extra -n if the plural already ends in -n or in -s: mit den Frauen, mit den Autos.
Masculine and neuter look the same: **-m** (dem, einem, meinem). Feminine ends in **-r** (der, einer, meiner).

head: Preposition
Meaning
Example
rows: mit meiner Freundin, mit dem Bus
bei meinen Eltern, bei einer Bank
aus der Türkei, aus dem Haus

items.de: Ich fahre mit dem Bus.
items.en: I'm going by bus.

items.de: Ich arbeite bei einer Bank.
items.en: I work at a bank.

items.de: Das Geschenk ist von meinem Bruder.
items.en: The present is from my brother.

items.de: Nach dem Essen trinken wir Kaffee.
items.en: After the meal we drink coffee.

items.de: Ich lerne seit drei Monaten Deutsch.
items.en: I've been learning German for three months.
items.note: seit + present tense for something that is still going on.

blocks.text: Learn the list as a chant: *aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu* — always dative!

blocks.why: der Bus is masculine; masculine dative is dem.

blocks.wrong: Ich wohne hier seit ein Jahr.
blocks.right: Ich wohne hier seit einem Jahr.
blocks.why: seit takes the dative: das Jahr → einem Jahr. And use the present tense, not a past form.

sections.heading: Short forms: zum, zur, beim, vom

blocks.text: These short forms are normal in everyday German — use them whenever you can. Only `zur` is feminine; all the others come from `dem` (masculine or neuter).

sections.heading: Wo? — in and an with the dative

blocks.text: When you answer **Wo?** (where?), `in` and `an` take the dative. `in` = inside a place, `an` = at / next to something (a station, a stop, the sea).

items.de: Wo bist du? – Im Supermarkt.
items.en: Where are you? – At the supermarket.

items.de: Die Kinder sind in der Schule.
items.en: The children are at school.

items.de: Ich warte an der Haltestelle.
items.en: I'm waiting at the bus stop.

items.de: Wo ist Anna? – Beim Arzt.
items.en: Where is Anna? – At the doctor's.

blocks.text: Wo? → `beim Arzt`, `im Kino`. Wohin? (where to?) → `zum Arzt`. (With Wohin?, in and an work differently — you'll learn that later.)
`nach` is also used with cities and most countries (no article): nach Wien, nach Spanien. With people and most other places use `zu`: zu meiner Freundin, zum Bahnhof.

blocks.why: Going home is a direction (Wohin?) → nach Hause. zu Hause means at home.
With cities and countries without an article, use nach.

exercises.en: I'm going by bus.
exercises.explain: mit + dative; der Bus is masculine → dem Bus.

exercises.en: She comes from Turkey.
exercises.explain: aus + dative; die Türkei is feminine → der Türkei.

exercises.en: I'm going to the doctor today.
exercises.explain: der Arzt is masculine: zu + dem = zum.

exercises.en: In the evening I go home.
exercises.explain: Going home is a direction → nach Hause. zu Hause = at home.

exercises.q: Ich wohne seit drei ___ in Köln.
exercises.en: I've been living in Cologne for three years.
exercises.explain: seit + dative; in the dative plural the noun adds -n: Jahre → Jahren.

exercises.q: Ich wohne bei ___ Eltern. (meine Eltern → Dativ)
exercises.en: I live with my parents.
exercises.explain: bei + dative plural: meine → meinen (Eltern already ends in -n).

exercises.en: We buy bread at the supermarket.
exercises.explain: Wo? → in + dative: in dem Supermarkt = im Supermarkt.

exercises.q: Das Geschenk ist von ___ Freundin. (meine Freundin → Dativ)
exercises.en: The present is from my girlfriend.
exercises.explain: von + dative; feminine: meine → meiner.

exercises.en: I'm waiting at the station.
exercises.explain: Wo? → an + dative: an dem Bahnhof = am Bahnhof.

accept: Mit dem Zug fahre ich.
exercises.en: I'm going by train.
exercises.explain: mit + dative: der Zug → dem Zug. The verb is in position 2.

exercises.answer: Nach dem Kurs gehe ich nach Hause.
accept: Ich gehe nach dem Kurs nach Hause.
Nach Hause gehe ich nach dem Kurs.
exercises.en: After the course I go home.
exercises.explain: nach dem Kurs = after the course; nach Hause = home (direction). The verb gehe stays in position 2.

exercises.answer: Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch.
accept: Seit einem Jahr lerne ich Deutsch.
Deutsch lerne ich seit einem Jahr.
exercises.en: I've been learning German for a year.
exercises.explain: seit + dative: ein Jahr → einem Jahr; present tense because it is still going on.

title: Das Perfekt
title_en: The present perfect (talking about the past)
summary: You'll be able to talk about what you did in the past using haben or sein and the past participle, the way Germans normally do in conversation.
key_points: Perfekt = haben/sein in position 2 + Partizip II at the end: Ich habe Pizza gegessen.
Regular verbs: ge- + stem + -t (gemacht, gearbeitet); many irregular verbs: ge- … -en (gegessen, geschrieben).
Separable verbs put -ge- in the middle (eingekauft); -ieren, be- and ver- verbs have no ge- (studiert, bezahlt, verstanden).
Most verbs use haben; verbs of movement or change (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, aufstehen) plus sein and bleiben use sein.
In speech the Perfekt is the normal past — but for sein and haben people say war and hatte.

blocks.text: The Perfekt has two parts: a form of **haben** or **sein** in position 2 (the normal verb position) and the **Partizip II** (past participle) at the very **end** of the sentence. Everything else goes in between.

items.de: Ich habe gestern Pizza gegessen.
items.en: I ate pizza yesterday.

items.de: Hast du das Buch gelesen?
items.en: Have you read the book?

items.de: Ich habe das nicht verstanden.
items.en: I didn't understand that.

blocks.why: The participle always goes to the very end of the sentence.

sections.heading: Partizip II: regular and irregular verbs

blocks.text: **Regular verbs:** ge- + stem + -t. If the stem ends in -t or -d, add -et: arbeiten → gearbeit**et**. **Irregular verbs** usually end in -en, and some change their vowel — learn them like vocabulary.

items.de: Wir haben am Abend gekocht.
items.en: We cooked in the evening.

items.de: Er hat einen Kaffee getrunken.
items.en: He drank a coffee.

blocks.text: When you learn a new verb, learn its participle with it: *essen – gegessen*, *sehen – gesehen*. That saves you a lot of guessing later.

sections.heading: Separable verbs and verbs without ge-

blocks.text: With **separable verbs**, -ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: ein**ge**kauft. Verbs ending in **-ieren** and verbs starting with **be-** or **ver-** take **no ge-** at all.

blocks.why: With separable verbs, -ge- goes after the prefix: ein-ge-kauft.
Verbs ending in -ieren have no ge-.
Verbs with be- or ver- have no ge-.

blocks.text: Most verbs form the Perfekt with **haben**. Use **sein** with verbs of **movement** from A to B and verbs of **change** — and also with `sein` and `bleiben` themselves.

items.de: Wir sind nach Spanien geflogen.
items.en: We flew to Spain.

items.de: Bist du mit dem Bus gekommen?
items.en: Did you come by bus?

items.de: Ich bin heute um sechs Uhr aufgestanden.
items.en: I got up at six o'clock today.

sections.heading: Perfekt in everyday speech — but war and hatte

blocks.text: When Germans talk about the past, they normally use the Perfekt. The big exception is **sein** and **haben**: here people almost always use the simple past forms **war** and **hatte**.

title: Das Perfekt – vertieft
summary: You'll be able to form the Perfekt of many more irregular verbs, choose confidently between haben and sein, and handle separable, inseparable and -ieren verbs.
key_points: Many irregular participles follow vowel patterns: trinken – getrunken, schreiben – geschrieben, essen – gegessen.
sein is used for movement from A to B, for a change of state (einschlafen, aufwachen, werden) and for sein, bleiben and passieren.
Separable verbs put -ge- in the middle (eingekauft); inseparable verbs (be-, ver-, er-, ge- …) and -ieren verbs have no ge- (bekommen, verstanden, telefoniert).
Modal verbs: in conversation use the Präteritum (ich musste, ich konnte), not the Perfekt.

sections.heading: Irregular participles: learn them in groups

blocks.text: In A1 you learned that irregular verbs form the Partizip II with **ge- … -en**, often with a new vowel. The good news: many verbs share the same vowel pattern. If you know `trinken – getrunken`, you can guess `finden – gefunden`.

items.de: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel endlich gefunden.
items.en: I finally found my key.

items.de: Die Kinder haben ein Lied gesungen.
items.en: The children sang a song.

items.de: Hast du heute schon etwas gegessen?
items.en: Have you eaten anything yet today?

items.de: Ich habe gestern mit meinem Chef gesprochen.
items.en: I spoke to my boss yesterday.

items.de: Sie hat Blumen mitgebracht.
items.en: She brought flowers.

blocks.text: Learn new irregular verbs in their group, e.g. *i → u: trinken, finden, singen*. Saying the three participles out loud together (*getrunken, gefunden, gesungen*) makes them stick.

blocks.why: trinken is irregular (i → u): getrunken. Only regular verbs end in -t.
denken is a mixed verb: new vowel and -t ending → gedacht.

sections.heading: haben or sein? The rules in detail

blocks.text: Most verbs use **haben**. Use **sein** in three cases: (1) **movement** from A to B, (2) a **change of state** — something starts or ends, e.g. you fall asleep or wake up, (3) the special verbs `sein`, `bleiben` and `passieren`.

head: Group
Verbs
Example
rows: gehen, fahren, fliegen, laufen, reisen, umziehen, einsteigen

items.de: Ich bin heute um sieben Uhr aufgewacht.
items.en: I woke up at seven o'clock today.

items.de: Mein Bruder ist Arzt geworden.
items.en: My brother became a doctor.

items.de: Wir sind im Sommer umgezogen.
items.en: We moved house in the summer.

blocks.why: schlafen is a state, not a change → haben. Only einschlafen (to fall asleep) is a change → ist eingeschlafen.
passieren always takes sein.

blocks.text: If a movement verb has an accusative object, it takes **haben**: *Ich **habe** meinen Vater zum Bahnhof gefahren* (I drove my father). Also: in southern Germany and Austria people say *ich bin gesessen/gestanden/gelegen* — in standard German it's *ich habe gesessen*.

**Separable** prefixes (an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, zu-, fern- …) are stressed and take -ge- in the middle. **Inseparable** prefixes (be-, ver-, er-, ent-, emp-, ge-, zer-) are never stressed and the participle has **no ge-**. Verbs ending in **-ieren** also have no ge-.

items.de: Ich habe gestern meine Oma angerufen.
items.en: I phoned my grandma yesterday.

items.de: Ich habe ein Paket bekommen.
items.en: I received a parcel.

items.de: Entschuldigung, ich habe deinen Namen vergessen.
items.en: Sorry, I've forgotten your name.

items.de: Sie hat mir von ihrer Reise erzählt.
items.en: She told me about her trip.

items.de: Wir haben im Urlaub viel fotografiert.
items.en: We took lots of photos on holiday.

blocks.text: Listen for the stress: **EIN**kaufen → ein**ge**kauft, but be**KOM**men → bekommen. And careful: `bekommen` means *to get/receive*, not *to become* (that's `werden`).

blocks.why: be- is an inseparable prefix → no ge-. The participle looks like the infinitive.

blocks.text: Modal verbs do have a Perfekt (*ich habe arbeiten müssen*), but it is complicated and rare in conversation. Germans normally use the short **Präteritum** forms instead: `ich musste`, `ich konnte`, `ich wollte`. You'll learn all the forms in the next chapter.

items.de: Gestern musste ich lange arbeiten.
items.en: Yesterday I had to work late.

items.de: Ich war müde, aber ich habe noch gekocht.
items.en: I was tired, but I still cooked.
items.note: war (Präteritum) + habe gekocht (Perfekt) — a typical mix

blocks.why: For modal verbs, use the Präteritum in everyday German.
